newsitem.title: UK: London forex market sees steady HK dlr under China.
newsitem.headline: London forex market sees steady HK dlr under China.

text.p: The Hong Kong dollar is likely to avoid a handover hangover and the forex community will not even notice the former British colony's transfer to China, say London currency analysts.

Hong Kong and Chinese officials are both keen to maintain the current stability of the dollar and have long stressed the continuation of the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar and the independence of Hong Kong's monetary system from China.

"If the confidence in China isn't as good as it is now or if Hong Kong China doesn't run smoothly, then there will be more of a risk premium on Hong Kong assets which could pressure the currency peg," said one London-based currency analyst.
"But the foreign currency reserves of the Hong Kong authority are so massive they would crush any sort of speculative attack on the currency."
Defending the currency poses little problem for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the region's central bank, which sits on about U.S.$63 billion in foreign exchange reserves.
Furthermore, the monetary authority is also assured of support, if it asks for it, from the mainland's People's Bank of China (PBOC), which has U.S.$115 billion in reserves.

Some concerns have been raised that in the distant future, the willingness of one central bank to defend the other's currency in times of crisis or speculative attacks may become strained. But the current reserve levels of both central banks and the current mood of co-operation is seen offsetting that risk.

Another talking point is the Hong Kong dollar peg of 7.80 to the U.S. dollar. This has been in place since 1983 when discussions between China and Britain over Hong Kong started and is seen as the root of Hong Kong's stability and prosperity.

"It might not be as appropriate for Hong Kong to have a dollar peg if the balance of its trade and investment was more of a Chinese orientation," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International.
"For instance, if Hong Kong, China become inward looking as opposed to outward looking, then that dollar peg might be difficult to maintain."
But this is unlikely in the near future and would only become an issue with full convertibility of China's renminbi currency and as China's international trade and financial power expand.

"Until China's financial sector is able to face full square to international competition in financial services, the renminbi will remain closed to full convertibility and Hong Kong will continue to operate as the international financial sector footbridge both from and into China," said Chris Tinker, chief economist at Standard Chartered Bank.
Concerns that the Hong Kong dollar may be diluted by increasing amounts of Chinese currency circulating in Hong Kong are also seen as overstated.
The yuan, or renminbi, is only likely to be held for use on the mainland and analysts see yuan transactions in Hong Kong being relatively small.

"There is no problem whatsoever, there is a clear formula about how Hong Kong dollars are created, so there isn't any notion of anything ever going into disequilibrium," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.
The Hong Kong dollar has held relatively steady in the run-up to the June 30 handover and analysts see little change on the horizon from current trading bands.

So far, the arguments for a Hong Kong dollar crisis are academic, say analysts. Hong Kong has autonomous control of its monetary system for the next 50 years as laid down in agreements governing the colony's reversion to Chinese rule and analysts see little indication of any change in the present system.
